purpose: Teach agents as bounded work systems with goals, environment, observations, actions, plans, tools, state, evidence, evaluation, handoffs, coordination, interaction, stop conditions, recovery, and accountable humans.
staffSummary: Build M41 around one consequential utility situation and one decision: Choose between a fixed workflow, one agent, or multiple specialists, then define the planning pattern, tool and state boundary, handoff, disagreement, recovery, escalation, and human-decision contract. The learner must leave with a usable utility agent architecture, coordination, and recovery contract, not a collection of definitions.
openingSituation: Three agents produce separate recommendations, but they use different source versions and no person owns disagreement or the final decision.
learnerDecision: Choose between a fixed workflow, one agent, or multiple specialists, then define the planning pattern, tool and state boundary, handoff, disagreement, recovery, escalation, and human-decision contract.
analogy: A staffed incident room works because roles, evidence, handoffs, command, and the decision log are explicit. More people without coordination create noise.
learnerOutcomes: Explain Agents, Agentic Nests, and Orchestration in plain English and connect it to a real water, wastewater, stormwater, or One Water decision.

Distinguish workflow, agent, goal, environment, observation, action, plan, Reason and Act, tool, state, specialist, orchestrator, shared state, handoff, evaluation, retry, conflict, deadlock, recovery, escalation, and stop without using one term to hide several different jobs.
Analyze the module situation, identify missing evidence, and name the professional consequence of a weak decision.
Compare how the same question changes across drinking water, wastewater, stormwater, administration, engineering, finance, technology, and public leadership.

Evaluate sources, assumptions, limitations, permissions, and human authority using this boundary: Do not imply that planning text, multiple agents, perceived agency, or tool access creates independent truth, professional judgment, or operating authority. Preserve sources, permissions, cost limits, dissent, and human decision rights.
Create a usable utility agent architecture, coordination, and recovery contract with evidence, roles, limits, review steps, and the next accountable action.
Defend the recommendation to Foundation, Practitioner, and Leader audiences while keeping disagreement and uncertainty visible.
curriculumOutcomes: Give Agents, Agentic Nests, and Orchestration one clear learning job inside Building AI Systems.
Connect the module to a consequential decision and the utility agent architecture, coordination, and recovery contract.
Preserve current content, proposals, enhancements, and contributor records by stable identifier.
Separate verified evidence, Hardeep positions, expert interpretation, instructional scenarios, and unresolved questions.
Create an explicit bridge to the preceding and following modules without duplicating their work.
marketingOutcomes: Describe the practical value as helping a learner make and explain this decision: Choose between a fixed workflow, one agent, or multiple specialists, then define the planning pattern, tool and state boundary, handoff, disagreement, recovery, escalation, and human-decision contract.
Name the utility agent architecture, coordination, and recovery contract as the visible result of the module.
Do not promise savings, compliance, certification, safety, performance, implementation success, or career outcomes without separately approved evidence.
requiredWorkProduct: utility agent architecture, coordination, and recovery contract
definitionOfDone: The learner explains the core distinctions, completes the required evidence and decision activities, passes distributed checks, saves a complete utility agent architecture, coordination, and recovery contract, and names the next accountable action.
scopeBoundary: Do not imply that planning text, multiple agents, perceived agency, or tool access creates independent truth, professional judgment, or operating authority. Preserve sources, permissions, cost limits, dissent, and human decision rights.
researchQuestions: What must an intelligent newcomer understand about Agents, Agentic Nests, and Orchestration before using it in utility work?

Which sources can support the distinctions among workflow, agent, goal, environment, observation, action, plan, Reason and Act, tool, state, specialist, orchestrator, shared state, handoff, evaluation, retry, conflict, deadlock, recovery, escalation, and stop?

What evidence would allow a practitioner to make this decision: Choose between a fixed workflow, one agent, or multiple specialists, then define the planning pattern, tool and state boundary, handoff, disagreement, recovery, escalation, and human-decision contract.
Which failure modes, counterexamples, and edge conditions could make the utility agent architecture, coordination, and recovery contract misleading?
How does the question change across drinking water, wastewater, stormwater, reuse, finance, engineering, administration, technology, and public accountability?
Which actions require qualified operator, engineer, water-quality, cybersecurity, privacy, legal, procurement, records, finance, accessibility, or executive review?

Which claims remain outside the module boundary: Do not imply that planning text, multiple agents, perceived agency, or tool access creates independent truth, professional judgment, or operating authority. Preserve sources, permissions, cost limits, dissent, and human decision rights.

acceptedExpansions.title: Agents, goals, environments, and perceived agency
acceptedExpansions.recommendation: Give learners a precise model for what an agent observes, what it may do, what goal it is pursuing, what environment it operates in, and why people can perceive more intelligence or authority than the system has.
acceptedExpansions.description: Give learners a precise model for what an agent observes, what it may do, what goal it is pursuing, what environment it operates in, and why people can perceive more intelligence or authority than the system has.
learningObjectives: Distinguish a model response, deterministic workflow, bounded agent, and multi-agent work system.
Specify a task using goal, performance measure, environment, observations, allowed actions, state, and stop conditions.
Compare predictable, uncertain, observable, partially observable, static, and changing environments.
Identify language and interface choices that cause people to overstate agency, understanding, or authority.
Create a utility agent environment and authority specification.
acceptedExpansions.workProduct: utility agent environment and authority specification
acceptedExpansions.evidenceBoundary: The academic agent model is a design lens. It does not grant an artificial intelligence system legal, professional, or operating authority.

subtopics.title: Goals, performance measures, and goal complexity
Observations, allowed actions, state, and tools
Human authority, prohibited action, and stop

acceptedExpansions.title: Planning, Reason and Act, reflection, and agentic retrieval
acceptedExpansions.recommendation: Compare fixed workflows with planning patterns that alternate reasoning, tool use, observation, evaluation, revision, and stop. Make observable evidence and control more important than hidden reasoning text.
acceptedExpansions.description: Compare fixed workflows with planning patterns that alternate reasoning, tool use, observation, evaluation, revision, and stop. Make observable evidence and control more important than hidden reasoning text.
learningObjectives: Compare fixed workflow, plan-and-execute, Reason and Act, reflection, and agentic retrieval patterns.
Trace the observable goal, plan, action, tool result, evidence, evaluation, adjustment, and stop for one task.
Choose the least complicated planning pattern that can satisfy the utility task and consequence boundary.
Identify endless-loop, tool-selection, stale-evidence, plan-drift, and false-completion failures.
Create and test a governed agent plan and trace.
acceptedExpansions.evidenceBoundary: Do not expose private hidden reasoning or treat a generated reasoning narrative as proof. Evaluate observable actions, sources, tool results, and outcomes.

subtopics.title: Classical plan, language-model plan, and fixed workflow
Agentic retrieval and iterative source refinement
Evaluation, retry budget, escalation, and stop

acceptedExpansions.title: Multi-agent coordination, conflict, cost, and failure
acceptedExpansions.recommendation: Teach multiple agents as a coordinated work system with explicit roles, communication, shared state, arbitration, evidence, cost, and accountable human decision. More agents can create more failure as easily as more capability.
acceptedExpansions.description: Teach multiple agents as a coordinated work system with explicit roles, communication, shared state, arbitration, evidence, cost, and accountable human decision. More agents can create more failure as easily as more capability.
learningObjectives: Choose among one workflow, one agent, and multiple specialist agents for a bounded utility task.
Design roles, messages, shared state, source versions, handoffs, arbitration, escalation, and final human authority.
Identify duplication, disagreement, stale state, deadlock, cascading error, excessive cost, and false consensus.
Use basic cooperation, incentive, and conflict reasoning without implying that agents are independent professionals.
Create and test a multi-agent coordination and recovery contract.
acceptedExpansions.evidenceBoundary: Multiple agents do not create independent truth, professional judgment, or legal authority. Preserve source versions, permissions, cost limits, dissent, and human decision rights.

subtopics.title: Shared state, source versions, and conflict
Deadlock, cascading failure, duplicated work, and cost multiplication
Human command, incident response, and final decision
